title: Tennis Says: Same Big Prize Money for Women and Men
summary:
Imagine winning a big tennis match — and finding out the prize money is smaller just because you're a girl. That's been the story in some tennis events for years. Now, that's changing.

The Women's Tennis Association (WTA) started in 1973 to help women's tennis grow. On Wednesday, it announced that from next year, women and men will get equal prize money at all combined 1,000 events. Those are the biggest tournaments outside the four Grand Slams. Some events, like Indian Wells and Miami, already paid equally. But the Italian Open, Canadian Open and Cincinnati Open will now catch up too.

"Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1,000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis," said WTA chair Valerie Camillo.

Players will also get a bit more free time. They now have to play fewer WTA 500 events — four instead of six. American star Jessica Pegula said the changes give players more power to plan their own seasons. That's a big win for everyone.
why_it_matters: It shows that girls and boys, women and men, should get the same reward for the same work, which is a fairness idea that matters at school, in sports and later at jobs.

background_read: The four Grand Slams are the biggest tennis tournaments in the world: the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the U.S. Open.
The U.S. Open was the first of them to pay women and men the same prize money, way back in the 1970s, and Wimbledon was the last one to change, in the 2000s.
Billie Jean King (a famous American tennis star) helped start the Women's Tennis Association in 1973 and spent years speaking up for equal pay for women players.
Article_Structure: WHO: The Women's Tennis Association, its chair Valerie Camillo, and players like American star Jessica Pegula.
WHAT: The WTA announced that from next year women and men will get equal prize money at all combined 1,000 tournaments, and players will have to play fewer WTA 500 events.
WHERE: At tennis tournaments around the world, including the Italian Open, the Canadian Open and the Cincinnati Open.
WHY: So women players are paid the same as men, and so players have more power to plan their own seasons.
